newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German firms cheered, price pressure eases.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German firms cheered, price pressure eases.

text.p: Business sentiment improved sharply in west Germany last month, while forward-looking indicators suggest inflation pressures remain very subdued, according to data released on Thursday.

While firms in the east of the country were slightly less optimistic for the future, a survey by the Ifo economic research institute showed west Germany's business climate index jumped to 94.7 in April from 92.6 in March.
Analysts said the Ifo data showed a healthier economic environment which would continue to improve this year.

"This is a really good number (which) fits better with the economic indicators we have already seen in the first quarter in production and incoming orders," said Uwe Angenendt, economist at BHF Bank in Frankfurt.
He said that in coming months, he expected more favourable news on the German economy.

Gernot Nerb, senior economist at Salomon Brothers said he thought Germany's export sector, which has blossomed in recent months as a result of a sharp dpereciation of the deutschemark, had led sentiment higher.
"I would say that mainly the export sector has boosted the index because construction and retailing remains very sluggish," he told Reuters Financial Television.
April M3 data, released earlier by the Bundesbank, showed a sharp drop in money supply growth aided by strengthening capital formation.

The Bundesbank said the headline M3 rate, which compares annualised M3 expansion with the average level in the final quarter of 1996, grew at a slower rate of 6.7 percent in April versus 8.3 percent in March.

Analysts said that with Germans growing nervous about the future amid talk of tax, pension and welfare reforms and concerns about the imminent single currency, higher capital formation -- when private sector savers park excess cash in long-term accounts -- had added the M3's slowdown.
They also said capital flows abroad and a reduction in public sector debt levels contributed to the easing.

Despite being well below market expectations -- and coming within an inch of the Bundebank's 3.5 to 6.5 percent M3 target range -- economists said the money supply numbers would not move the Bundesbank on monetary policy.
"The slowdown in M3 will bolster the Bundesbank's viewpoint that future inflation pressure are benign. It will not, however, prompt any adjustment in policy," HSBC economists said in a research note.

Indeed, Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert said in a speech in Leipzig on Thursday that recent M3 developments still said very little about whether the central bank's target range could be reached this year.
Sievert said that he saw no current leeway for an easing in German monetary policy but added that there was also no reason to consider a move to tighten credit in the near future.
German official interest rates have been on hold since August last year.
